hook.text: Three CDN providers serve most of the web. If one fails, millions of sites go down. Good design?

buildup.text: Centralization brings efficiency: shared infra, expert ops, low cost. But it creates concentration risk.

discovery.text: The original internet was decentralized — no single point of failure. Economic forces reversed that.

twist.text: Multi-CDN strategies exist but are complex and costly. Most companies pick one provider for simplicity.

climax.text: The 2021 outages at Fastly, Akamai, and Facebook sparked real action on multi-provider redundancy.

punchline.text: Convenience drives centralization. Outages drive decentralization.

quiz.question: What risk does internet centralization create?
options: A single provider failure can take down millions of sites
Websites become slower for all users

details.summary: The internet was designed as a decentralized network, but modern usage concentrates traffic through a few cloud providers, CDNs, and DNS services. This centralization creates correlated failure risk where one provider's outage takes down thousands of apparently independent services.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding centralization risk explains why unrelated websites go down together. The internet's resilience depends on maintaining diversity in infrastructure providers.
takeaways: The internet's original design was highly decentralized
Modern usage concentrates through few cloud and CDN providers
Centralization creates correlated failures across services

faq.question: Why has the internet become more centralized?
faq.answer: Economies of scale make large cloud providers cheaper and easier to use. CDNs improve performance. Managed DNS reduces operational burden. Each choice is rational individually, but collectively they concentrate the internet through a handful of providers.

faq.question: Can the internet become more decentralized again?
faq.answer: Multi-cloud strategies, edge computing, and decentralized protocols push back against centralization. But convenience and cost advantages keep driving concentration. The tension between efficiency and resilience is a fundamental and likely permanent trade-off.
